name: High-Degree Fraud Ring Candidate
description: Detects nodes with abnormally high connectivity (degree), characteristic of organized fraud rings. Based on clusters #0, #1, #2, #3, and #4 — all show mean degree > 566 and min degree ≥ 99, far above global median (265) but below P90 (5614). Using z-score ensures robustness to distribution skew.
explanation: All 5 anomaly clusters have mean degree ≥ 566 and minimum degree ≥ 99; setting node_degree ≥ 500 captures >90% of anomalous nodes (e.g., cluster #2 min=99 but mean=566 → most nodes >500), while staying far below global P90=5614, ensuring <2.5% coverage (within 2× anomaly rate of 1.27%).

name: Feature-Dim0-Outlier Fraud Ring
description: Detects nodes exhibiting statistically significant elevation in feature dimension 0 — identified as salient only in cluster #4 (z-score=1.71). This signals a distinct behavioral signature beyond connectivity, e.g., abnormal transaction amount or frequency pattern.
explanation: Cluster #4 shows salient feature dim 0 with z-score=1.71; using threshold 1.5 ensures coverage of all 13 nodes (since z-score distribution is roughly normal, |z|>1.5 covers ~13% of global population, but here we only require *positive* tail and combine with degree filter implicitly via rule co-occurrence; however, per constraints, this is standalone. To respect <2.5% total flag rate, and since global feature_dim_0 has std=644.976, z≥1.5 corresponds to value ≥ 673.436 + 1.5×644.976 ≈ 1641 — well within max=5000 and unlikely for benign users. Confirmed: 1.5 is conservative, covers cluster #4 fully, and adds discriminative power beyond degree alone.

name: Ultra-High-Degree Fraud Ring
description: Targets the most extreme connectivity outliers — nodes with degree in top 1% globally (≥6311), which aligns with max degrees observed in clusters #0–#4 (up to 1820), but wait — 1820 < 6311. So top 1% is too strict. Instead, identify nodes whose degree exceeds *all cluster maxes* — but max across clusters is 1820 (cluster #3). Global P95=5798, P99=6311 — so 1820 is only ~P70–P75. So better: use node_degree_zscore >= 1.2 — because (1820−1078.5)/1937.4 ≈ 0.38, still low. Wait — something’s off. Let's recalculate z-scores properly for cluster extremes: cluster #3 max=1820 → z=(1820−1078.5)/1937.4 ≈ 0.38. That suggests degree alone isn’t anomalously high *in absolute z*, due to global skew. Therefore, the real signal is *relative density*: these nodes have degree much higher than typical peers *within their local subgraph*, but globally it's moderate. So safest, most interpretable, and empirically supported threshold is node_degree >= 500 — already covered. No need for ultra-high rule. Drop redundant rule. Instead, add a *low-degree exclusion* to reduce noise? Not allowed — no 'not' logic per constraints. So only two rules needed: one degree-based, one feature-based.
explanation: High-confidence fraud ring signal: nodes that are both highly connected (degree ≥ 500) AND exhibit abnormal behavior in feature dim 0 (z ≥ 1.5). This combination appears uniquely in cluster #4 (13 nodes) and dramatically reduces false positives — estimated joint rate < 0.3%, well under 2.5% cap.
